title: Israeli Strikes in Gaza Kill 12, Including Family of Six, as Ceasefire Erodes
excerpt: Three separate airstrikes on Tuesday killed at least 12 Palestinians in Gaza, including a father, his wife, and four children whose home was set ablaze in the Sabra neighbourhood of Gaza City, as the nine-month-old ceasefire continues to fray.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Israeli airstrikes killed 12 Palestinians, including a family of six, in Gaza on Tuesday.
  • Over 1,160 Palestinians have died since the October 2025 ceasefire began, mostly civilians.
  • Israeli military claims to target militants, but civilian casualties continue to rise.
  • Diplomatic efforts for a ceasefire second phase have made minimal progress.
  • The broader conflict has resulted in over 73,000 Palestinian deaths since October 2023.

  • More than 1,160 Palestinians have been killed since a U.S.-backed ceasefire took effect in October 2025, according to Gaza health officials.
  • Mediation efforts by Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, and the United States have made little progress on a second phase of the truce deal requiring Hamas disarmament and Israeli withdrawals.

Family Killed as Home Burns in Pre-Dawn Strike

An Israeli airstrike struck a family home in the Sabra neighbourhood of Gaza City early Tuesday, killing Firas Al-Masri, his wife Salsabeel, and their three daughters and son, according to Palestinian health officials. The strike set the house ablaze, with rescue workers struggling to extinguish the fire and recover bodies wrapped in white shrouds, Reuters reported.

The Israeli military confirmed carrying out the strike, saying its target was a Hamas militant, and that it was still assessing the outcome. The military did not identify the militant or address the civilian casualties.

"We were unable to save our grandchildren and children from the flames and the devastation. Around five or six were martyred, most of them children and women, without mercy and without any prior warning."

— Abu Yusuf Al-Masri, father of Firas Al-Masri, speaking to Reuters
> **"Hamas does not typically disclose its losses."**

Abu Yusuf Al-Masri said the explosion struck while the family was asleep. Standing outside the charred remains of the house, he added: "There is no relative calm and there is no safe place, at all."

Tuesday's Death Toll Reaches 12

Later on Tuesday, two separate Israeli airstrikes targeted a vehicle in the central Gaza Strip and an association in Gaza City, killing at least six more people and wounding others, Palestinian medics said. The Israeli military did not immediately comment on either incident.

Since Friday, the Israeli military has said it killed four militants from Hamas and Islamic Jihad in four separate strikes, three of whom it claimed had taken part in the October 7, 2023 attack on southern Israel and had held hostages seized during the assault.

A Ceasefire in Name Only

The latest deaths push the toll since the October 2025 ceasefire past 1,160 Palestinians killed, mostly civilians, according to Gaza health officials. Hamas does not typically disclose its losses. Four Israeli soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza during the same period.

The truce halted full-scale military operations but has failed to stop near-daily Israeli strikes. Israel maintains it is targeting militants. Conflict monitor ACLED, a U.S.-based research group, reported that Israeli airstrikes against Hamas and other militants rose to more than 40 in June — the highest monthly total since the ceasefire began — with other strikes killing and injuring civilians, including women and children.

The broader toll of the war, which began with Hamas-led fighters attacking southern Israel on October 7, 2023, killing some 1,200 people and taking roughly 250 hostages, now stands at over 73,000 Palestinians killed, according to Gaza health officials. Nearly all of Gaza's 2 million residents have been compressed into a narrow strip of coastal land, living in makeshift tents or damaged buildings under dire conditions.

Stalled Diplomacy and the Hamas Governance Gambit

Mediators including Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, and the United States have been pushing to advance President Donald Trump's plan for ending the conflict, which calls for Hamas disarmament and full Israeli military withdrawal. Progress has been minimal.

Territory Israel Aims to Occupy

Earlier this month, Hamas announced it would dissolve its government in Gaza and hand authority to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), a technocratic body envisioned under the ceasefire plan. The Board of Peace, created to advance the agreement, responded coolly, saying it would wait for "actions, not promises" and calling on Hamas to disarm.

Muhammad Shehada, a Gaza expert at the European Council on Foreign Relations, described the Hamas announcement as an attempt to "talk over Netanyahu's head" and appeal directly to Trump. But he cautioned that the move likely comes too late, noting that "Israel still has ultimate control over everything in Gaza."

The NCAG has remained in Cairo, unable to enter the territory or exercise any governing authority. Israel's military has instead seized more of the strip, with a stated goal of occupying approximately 70 percent of the territory, forcing Gaza's population into an ever-shrinking area.

India's Position and the Diaspora

India has continued to call for a two-state solution and an immediate end to civilian casualties while maintaining diplomatic ties with both Israel and Palestine. For the Indian diaspora, particularly the sizeable community in the Gulf states living alongside Palestinian populations, the continued violence presents both a humanitarian concern and a geopolitical reality that shapes regional stability. Indian workers in Qatar, the UAE, and other Gulf nations that serve as mediators have a direct stake in the region's trajectory.

What's Next

With the ceasefire's second phase stalled and daily strikes continuing, the near-term outlook for Gaza remains bleak. The Board of Peace has held what it called "highly productive" meetings in Cyprus, preparing for the NCAG to assume control "once the right conditions are met," though those conditions remain undefined.

For families like the Al-Masris, the diplomacy is an abstraction measured against an immediate, irreversible reality. As international mediators push for incremental progress, the gap between the ceasefire agreement on paper and the violence on the ground continues to widen.
